lesson.2_1.title: Bank accounts and the words on your passbook
lesson.2_1.gut.prompt: You are given ₹3,000 as a gift. Where does it go?
lesson.2_1.gut.bridge: A bank account is your money's safe home. Let's learn the words printed on it.
lesson.2_1.gut.a.label: In a drawer at home
lesson.2_1.gut.a.result: It is close by, and easy to spend. It earns nothing, and it is gone if it is lost or stolen.
lesson.2_1.gut.b.label: In a bank account
lesson.2_1.gut.b.result: It is recorded in your name and earns a little interest. You can still take it out when you need it.
lesson.2_1.gut.c.label: Spend it this week
lesson.2_1.gut.c.result: Fun now. Nothing is left for the next thing you want or need.
lesson.2_1.c1.text: Cash at home can be lost, stolen or spent without a plan. Money in a bank is recorded in your name.
lesson.2_1.c2.text: A savings account keeps your money at a bank and pays you a little for keeping it there. That payment is called interest.
lesson.2_1.c2.reveal.prompt: In this game a savings account pays 3% a year. What does ₹3,000 earn in a month?
lesson.2_1.c2.reveal.answer: About ₹7.50. Small, but a drawer pays ₹0.
lesson.2_1.c3.text: To open an account the bank must know who you are. That check is called KYC: your identity and address documents.
lesson.2_1.c4.text: You name a nominee: the person who receives the money if something happens to you.
lesson.2_1.c5.text: A passbook or statement lists every rupee that came in and went out. The IFSC is the code of your bank branch. People need it to send you money.
lesson.2_1.c5.sort.balance: How much is in the account now
lesson.2_1.c5.sort.branch: The code a friend needs to send you money
lesson.2_1.c5.sort.interest: How much interest the bank paid you
lesson.2_1.c5.sort.feedback: A statement is the diary of your account. Read it every month.
lesson.2_1.c6.text: Some accounts ask you to keep a minimum balance. Fall below it and the bank takes a charge. Student accounts often ask for none.
lesson.2_1.c7.text: Money in a bank is also insured up to a limit set by law. Deposit insurance in India is run by the DICGC.
lesson.2_1.q1.prompt: What is interest on a savings account?
lesson.2_1.q1.right: Yes. The bank pays you interest for keeping money with it.
lesson.2_1.q1.wrong: Interest is what the bank pays you. The branch code is the IFSC, and a fee is a charge.
lesson.2_1.q1.o1: A fee you pay the bank every month
lesson.2_1.q1.o2: Money the bank pays you for keeping your money there
lesson.2_1.q2.prompt: A nominee is the person who receives your money if something happens to you.
lesson.2_1.q2.right: Correct. Naming a nominee saves your family a lot of trouble.
lesson.2_1.q2.wrong: It's true. The nominee is the person the bank pays if the account holder dies.
lesson.2_1.q3.prompt: Your account has a ₹1,000 minimum balance. Your balance drops to ₹400. What can happen?
lesson.2_1.q3.right: Right. Falling below the minimum balance can cost you a charge.
lesson.2_1.q3.wrong: The bank can take a charge when you go below the minimum balance. Check this rule before you choose an account.
lesson.2_1.q3.o2: The bank can take a charge
lesson.2_1.effect: Your Savings account opens. Money you move into it earns 3% a year, a little every month.
lesson.2_2.title: Cards, UPI and the safe-payment rules
lesson.2_2.gut.prompt: A message says: "Your ₹500 refund is waiting. Enter your UPI PIN to receive it." What do you do?
lesson.2_2.gut.bridge: Paying by phone is quick. A few rules keep it safe.
lesson.2_2.gut.a.label: Enter the PIN
lesson.2_2.gut.a.result: The money leaves your account. A PIN is never needed to receive money.
lesson.2_2.gut.b.label: Ignore the message
lesson.2_2.gut.b.result: Nothing is lost. A real refund arrives by itself.
lesson.2_2.gut.c.label: Ask an adult or call the bank
lesson.2_2.gut.c.result: A good habit: pause, then check with someone you trust.
lesson.2_2.c1.text: There are many ways to pay without cash. Each one has a rule that keeps your money safe.
lesson.2_2.c2.text: A debit card spends your own money, straight from your account. A credit card spends the bank's money, and you must repay it.
lesson.2_2.c2.sort.feedback: Borrowed money always has to be repaid. Level 4 looks at what that costs.
lesson.2_2.c3.text: UPI moves money from one bank account to another in seconds, using a phone.
lesson.2_2.c4.text: Your UPI PIN is the secret number that approves a payment. You enter it only when you are sending money.
lesson.2_2.c4.reveal.prompt: Do you ever need your PIN to receive money?
lesson.2_2.c4.reveal.answer: Never. Money sent to you simply arrives. A PIN only ever sends money out.
lesson.2_2.c5.text: An OTP is a one-time code sent to your phone to approve one action. The CVV is the three-digit code on the back of a card. Nobody needs either of them from you: not a bank, a shop or a helpline.
lesson.2_2.c6.text: Two common tricks: a "collect request" dressed up as a refund, and a QR code "to receive a prize". Approving a request or scanning a code sends money out.
lesson.2_2.q1.prompt: You must enter your UPI PIN to receive money.
lesson.2_2.q1.right: Correct, it's false. A PIN only ever sends money.
lesson.2_2.q1.wrong: It's false. Receiving needs nothing from you. If a screen asks for your PIN, money is about to leave.
lesson.2_2.q2.prompt: A caller says he is from your bank and asks for the OTP "to stop a wrong payment". What do you do?
lesson.2_2.q2.right: Yes. The OTP is what approves the payment. Hang up and call the official number.
lesson.2_2.q2.wrong: Never share an OTP or CVV. Hang up and call the number printed on your passbook or card.
lesson.2_2.q2.o2: Hang up and call the bank's official number yourself
lesson.2_2.q2.o3: Send him your card's CVV instead
lesson.2_2.q3.prompt: Which card spends the bank's money, which you repay later?
lesson.2_2.q3.right: Right. A credit card is borrowing. A debit card uses your own balance.
lesson.2_2.q3.wrong: A credit card spends the bank's money and you repay it. A debit card spends your own.
lesson.2_2.effect: Your first Scam Alert is on its way, and your scam-safety record starts. Every alert you handle well adds to it.
lesson.2_3.title: How banks use your money
lesson.2_3.gut.prompt: You have ₹3,000 to keep. Account A: no minimum balance, 2.5% interest a year. Account B: 3.5% a year, but ₹150 every three months if your balance is under ₹5,000. Which one suits ₹3,000?
lesson.2_3.gut.bridge: Why does a bank pay you at all? Follow the money.
lesson.2_3.gut.a.label: Account A
lesson.2_3.gut.a.result: About ₹75 of interest in a year, and no charges.
lesson.2_3.gut.b.label: Account B
lesson.2_3.gut.b.result: About ₹105 of interest in a year, but ₹600 in charges, because ₹3,000 is under the minimum.
lesson.2_3.gut.c.label: Read the charges first
lesson.2_3.gut.c.result: A useful habit. The higher rate only helps once you can keep the minimum balance.
lesson.2_3.c1.text: A bank does not lock your money in a room. It lends most of it to other people and businesses.
lesson.2_3.c2.text: Borrowers pay the bank interest. The bank passes a part of that on to you. That is why your savings earn something.
lesson.2_3.c2.reveal.prompt: A bank pays savers 3% and charges borrowers 10%. Where does the gap go?
lesson.2_3.c2.reveal.answer: It pays the bank's costs and its profit. That gap is how a bank earns.
lesson.2_3.c3.text: You can still take your money out, because not everyone needs their money on the same day. The bank also keeps a part aside.
lesson.2_3.c4.text: Accounts differ in three ways: the interest they pay, the minimum balance they ask for, and the charges they take.
lesson.2_3.c4.sort.prompt: Does it add to your money or take from it?
lesson.2_3.c4.sort.minFee: A charge for a low balance
lesson.2_3.c4.sort.feedback: Read the charges as carefully as the interest rate.
lesson.2_3.c5.text: With ₹3,000: Account A earns about ₹75 a year. Account B earns about ₹105, then takes ₹600 in charges. A higher rate can still leave you with less.
lesson.2_3.c6.text: Which account fits depends on how much you can keep in it. There is no single answer for everyone.
lesson.2_3.q1.prompt: Why can a bank pay you interest?
lesson.2_3.q1.right: Yes. Borrowers pay more than savers earn. The gap runs the bank.
lesson.2_3.q1.wrong: A bank lends deposits out. Borrowers pay it interest, and a part of that comes to you.
lesson.2_3.q1.o1: The government gives it free money
lesson.2_3.q1.o2: It lends your money out and earns interest from borrowers
lesson.2_3.q2.prompt: The account with the highest interest rate always leaves you with the most money.
lesson.2_3.q2.right: Correct, it's false. Charges can take more than the extra interest gives.
lesson.2_3.q2.wrong: It's false. A low-balance charge can be bigger than the extra interest. Look at both.
lesson.2_3.q3.prompt: Account B pays about ₹105 of interest on ₹3,000 in a year and takes ₹600 in charges. What happens to your money?
lesson.2_3.q3.right: Right. ₹600 out is more than ₹105 in.
lesson.2_3.q3.wrong: It shrinks: the charges (₹600) are bigger than the interest (₹105).
lesson.2_3.effect: You choose which account holds your savings. The interest and any charges show up every month.
